messages.subject: Mapping occupancy from colext
messages.subject_clean: Mapping occupancy from colext
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to produce a map of predicted occupancy at the end of my study, which consists of 64 seasons with 8 visits per season. Data was collected from 31 sites in one reserve.

I have a fitted model that looks like:

> fm<- colext(~DfW + NDVI + DfR + DfF + TPI, ~DfW + NDVI + DfR + DfF + TPI + date + I(date^2), ~DfW + NDVI + DfR + DfF + TPI + date + I(date^2), ~TPI + time,UMF)

I think I have obtained occupancy predictions (Psi) for the last season by using

> yz=fm@projected[2, 64, ].

I would now like to map the probability of occupancy across the entire reserve based on the final Psi values for each site. I think I should be using something like the code in Chandler (2017) 'Modelling and mapping species distribution':

> E.psi <- predict(fm.occu, type="state", newdata=ef)
> plot(E.psi, axes=FALSE, col=terrain.colors(100))

I have a raster stack 'ef', but I'm not sure how to plug in the correct Psi values?

Any help would be greatly appreciated,
Thanks,
Oliver Metcalf

messages.body_plain:
Just to second Marc Kery's observation that the MLE's for abundance and detection are infinity and zero.

Because the counts are low in this data (0, 1, and 2) one can construct the exact log of the likelihood:

logL = -18 p (3 + (-3 + p) p) lambda - Log[4] + 26 Log[1 - p] +
           22 Log[p] + 16 Log[lambda] + 4 Log[1 - (-1 + p)^3 lambda]] +
           Log[1 + (-1 + p)^3 lambda (-3 + (-1 + p)^3 lambda)]

All of the solutions for when the partial derivatives of logL with respect to lambda and p equal zero do not satisfy 0 < p < 1.  Therefore the MLE is on the "boundary" which in this case is infinity and zero for lambda and p, respectively.  (I've attached the Mathematica code for constructing the log likelihood and finding the solutions for when the partial derivatives equal zero.

If you had a justifiable prior on lambda and p, you could do better (but maybe not much better).

Jim

After looking at the observed vs. predicted values I found that the model gives me different predicted values when the transect length is different. For example I get
predicted values for:

Site 1 year 1 Habitat forest
Site 1 year 1 Habitat coffee
Site 2 year 1 Habitat forest
Site 2 year 1 Habitat coffee
Site 3 year 1 Habitat forest
Site 3 year 1 Habitat coffee     and so in for years 2 and 3.

Let's say most of my transects in Site 1 Year 1 Habitat forest are 500, but there is one that is 300 m so the model gives me a different predicted values for that transect.
I read related posts in this group but could't find a solution. I'll appreciate if someone can help me out.

Many thanks
Ana

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I used a stratified random sampling design. 5 regions (strata) with 9 randomly selected sampling sites within each region, for a total of 45 sampling sites. Each site was sampled for a 7 night period 4 times each year (corresponding to bat reproductive cycles) during the 3 year study. This provided 84 discrete observations for each of the 45 sampling sites (7x4x3 = 84).

Each sampling site was categorized by habitat type - tree (1) or shrub (0). I am running a multiple season analysis and I’m interested in looking at the effect of habitat and region on occupancy, and the effect of habitat, reproductive cycle, and region on detection probability. None of the models of these covariates taken individually performed the best in single parameter models ((psi(.) gamma(.) epsilon(.)p(cycle)). However, combinations of covariates did ((psi(.) gamma(.) epsilon(.)p(cycle*region).

I have the following questions

In order to look at the above mentioned effects on psi and p do I need to use the best model that incorporates all the covariates of interest (including those for gamma and epsilon) or do I run the best performing psi model separately from the best p model to see these effects?

Would I run a GOF test first? If so is the parboot() function appropriate? Others on this forum (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!search/GOF$20colext/unmarked/LvLJj2xoe1s/uUch5vJKRlQJ) have suggested that there may be limitations to GOF tests for binary data such as mine but I could have misinterpreted that.

Is a likelihood ratio test (LRT) appropriate for determining effects of these covariates on psi or p for colext models or is there another one? I’ve seen others on this forum using it to test the null hypothesis instead of the Wald z test that the summary gives you but only with occu.

In addition to knowing how covariates affect psi and p I also want to present the best estimate of occupancy for each site and region. Would I use ranef() and the best, fully parameterized model to do this?

Is Unmarked sufficient to look for differences in occupancy and detectability among regions and/or reproductive cycles? Bayesian Analysis has been suggested as a more robust method but as I am not a statistician I am unclear about this type of analysis. Am I correct in thinking that detecting effects of covariates on occupancy and detection probabilities is a different process from detecting actual differences in those parameters?

I think I may be confusing two different study goals with different approaches. I'm still researching when to use predict() and ranef() and how to best use them in this study. Any help is much appreciated. I really value the unmarked community’s input and have really benefitted from the contributors in the past. Thanks in advance.

Cheers,

Rachel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Joaquin,

You will have to organize detection data in a “balanced” way, i.e., fill up the missing occasions in year 1 with NAs. Hence, the top of your detection data, as you must supply it for unmarked, will look like this:

1-NA-NA-NA-0-1-0

0-NA-NA-NA-0-0-0

.....

Then, by telling unmarked that you have two years and 4 occasions each, things will be filled in in the right way. You should then NOT fit models where p is made year-dependent, because you must make p identical across years in order to inform p in year 1 by the information coming from year 2.

As for the types of covariates, they can be somewhat confusing perhaps when you only have two occasions. In this case, one of the three types doesn’t make sense: you cannot fit yearly site-covariates in a study with only 2 primarly occasions, since yearly site-covariates are used to explain variation in the dynamic rate params (colonisation, extinction). But with only two primary occasions, you only have a single colonisation and a single extinction parameter, hence, you can only try to explain spatial, but not spatio-temporal variation in them. That’s done by fitting site covariates.

Best regards  --- Marc

    g = 1 - 1/(1 + exp(0.715)) = 0.671505
    e = 1 - 1/(1 + exp(-1.31)) = 0.2124868
    p = 1 - 1/(1 + exp (-0.433)) = 0.3934102

The occupancy probabilities for the remaining primary survey periods are

    psi2 = psi1*(1-e) + (1-psi1)*g = 0.787487
    psi3 = psi2*(1-e) + (1-psi2)*g = 0.76286
    psi4 = psi3*(1-e) + (1-psi3)*g = 0.760003
    .

There are functions in unmarked to get all of the above but I've just written the formulas to make it more explicit.

Dear Joaquin,

glad you get stuff into an unmarkedMultFrame.

But no, I was not suggesting to model your problem with occ. I think that it can be interesting to partition the change in occupancy between period 1 and 2 into the two components: colonisation and extinction. These are different processes and may be affected by different covariates.

But if you are not interested in these processes, you can simply stack the data, treat year as a factor and use occu to fit a static model. That's an alternative.

If you want to model colonisation/extinction dynamics then you must note that you cannot fit a yearly site-covariate into the colo or the ext models, only site covariates work. With two primary periods, you only have a single parameter each for colo and extinction and hence all you can model there is spatial heterogeneity. This is taken account for by a site covariate.

Re. those covariates that you have measured at both primary occasions: in the context of a model with colo and extinction I would think about what you know about these birds mechanistically. Is it the environmental conditions during the first or during the second primary occasion that seems more likely to affect colo or extinction ? Then take that. If you can't decide, then you could take the average and use that as a site covariate. Or, you specify these covariates for each year as a separate site covariate and fit each of them. But check first their correlation: if they're highly correlated (e.g., r > 0.6 or 0.7) then there is no use fitting them both.

Best regards  --- Marc

starts <-c(1.16699470,4.13455875,0.53512199,-1.28441477,  0, 0.18498429,-0.03367617)

model.2 <- colext(psiformula = ~y1.seed+y1.perch, # First-year occupancy
                  gammaformula = ~y2.perch , # Colonization
                  epsilonformula = ~ 1, # Extinction
                  pformula = ~ 1, # Detection

                  data = umf1, starts = starts)

Hi Rachel,

I was talking about years because it is a commonly used temporal scale, but it doesn't need to be the one used in the study (only if it makes sense). You are correct, you should have a look at the detection history in each primary period. Still, you seem to have a very high occupancy rate, so it is likely that the variability in your data would be due to the imperfect detection.

Note that if you have more than one primary period per year, then the estimates of the model will refer to the probabilities of extinction and colonisation for the periods spanned between primary periods.

Cheers

Pablo

I assume that the same sites are surveyed in both seasons.  If so, by design that imposes a dependency structure and that should be an integral part of the analysis.  colext can account for that where occu cannot.

While it is unlikely that the estimates and standard errors of occupancy probabilities for the 4 combinations will differ whether colext or occu is used, what is more likely to be different are the standard errors of the differences of like vegetation types between seasons.  In other words, you can really only appropriately compare veg types between seasons with measures of precision constructed with colext.

If the status of site is independent between seasons, then either colext or occu could be used.  But the catch is that you don’t know that.  Therefore, my recommendation is to use colext.

messages.body_plain:
I've posted here on this project previously, but a quick run down.  Ultimately, I'm trying to compare the occupancy of rats across islands in Palau with the relative abundance of a ground nesting bird (a species of megapode) to determine an effect (i.e., do rats effect megapodes).  Focusing here on rats, I established 10 transects across 10 islands, each transect consisting of 10 chew tags spaced appropriately.  Five of the islands are visited by tourists, the other five are not visited (off limits, essentially).  I'm also looking for effect of tourist presence on both rats and megapodes.  Due to logistical constraints, I only had the opportunity to run two survey replicates.  Thus, I have a total of 20 observations per island, across two replicates of 10 each.  Pretty small sample, all said and done.

I tried to model occupancy (occu function) of rats by island to acquire an estimate for each that I could then use in an island level GLM (Gaussian) comparing rats to megapodes on tourist an non-tourist islands.  When I employed the "predict" function for occupancy estimates and CI, I got this:

   Predicted           SE         lower     upper
1  0.9999983 4.114783e-04 2.824357e-201 1.0000000
2  0.5175645 1.637889e-01  2.287504e-01 0.7951014
3  0.7245876 1.502624e-01  3.755559e-01 0.9200569
4  0.7245876 1.502624e-01  3.755559e-01 0.9200569
5  0.6210613 1.605394e-01  3.009183e-01 0.8618855
6  0.9317151 9.883415e-02  3.937964e-01 0.9965229
7  1.0000000 2.632661e-05  0.000000e+00 1.0000000
8  1.0000000 3.904863e-05  0.000000e+00 1.0000000
9  1.0000000 3.904863e-05  0.000000e+00 1.0000000
10 1.0000000 3.904863e-05  0.000000e+00 1.0000000

Fairly uninformative CI, especially for islands 7-10, and I'm assuming this is because the predictions for these are boundary estimates.  I'm suspecting that this may also be due to my relative small sample sizes?  Is there any way to handle or correct these?  And, as the CI are not terribly useful and perhaps the result of sample size, I'm assuming that the predicted estimates for occupancy are not accurate and should not be relied upon (and should best not be used in the above mentioned GLM)???

One note, however.  Rows 1, 6, and 8-10 are tourist visited islands - and detections rates were notably far higher on those islands than those not visited, and correspondingly, Row 6 was the tourist visited island with the lowest detection rate.  The one exception to the trend of lower detection rates for non-tourist islands is Row 7, which is an island that had a history of past tourist pressure (I had to take what I could get in terms of islands for each category).  So, in short, although perhaps not the best results, these predicted estimates do appear to fit my raw data.

If there is anything else I can provide to assist with thoughts on this, please let me know and I'll post.

Thanks and cheers,
Paul
